main.text: It is proved that קאת kaath is the pelican and the heron, especially the starred heron, that is, the bittern.

For the Greeks, here and in the seventh verse of Psalm 101 (102 for the Hebrews), קאת kaath is the pelican. So too for Jerome in the passage of the Psalm, although elsewhere he renders it onocrotalus. Onkelos [=Targum Onkelos] and the Samaritan retain the Hebrew word. In its place Jonathan [=Targum Jonathan] and the Syriac have ܩܩܐ [קקא] kaka; Erpenianus [=the Arabic version edited by Thomas Erpenius (Pentateuch 1622; New Testament 1616)] has القوق [al-qūq] alkuk, and the other القيق [al-qīq] alkik. Nor do the Talmudic writers say otherwise. Thus the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Cholin, ch. 3, fol. 63a: אמר רב יהודה קאת זו הקוק, R. Judah said: Kaath is kuk. So also R. Ishmael in the Jerusalem Talmud. And for קוק kuk some write קיק kik. Accordingly, in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 2, fol. 21a, Rabbi Samuel, asked where שמן קיק, oil of kik, comes from, answers thus: שאלתי נהו לכל נחותי ימא ואמרו לי עוף אחד יש בכרכי הים וקיק שמו, I asked this very thing of all those who go down to the sea, and they told me that a bird named kik is found in the coastal towns. And Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] in his Lexicon cites the passages of the Talmud as if he had read kik everywhere. His words are: ובתלמוד אמר רב יהודה קאת זה הקיק ובתלמוד ירושלמי תני רבי ישמעאל קאת זה הקיק, And in the Talmud Rabbi Judah said that kaath is kik. Also in the Jerusalem Talmud Rabbi Ishmael taught that kaath is kik. We have noted that the Arabic paraphrasts also write it both ways. Yet among them قوق [qūq] kuk and قيق [qīq] kik differ greatly. For قوق [qūq] kuk is طاير ماي طويل العنق [ṭāyir māʾī ṭawīl al-ʿunuq], a water bird with a long neck. So Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī] and Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān] define it, from the book entitled العباب [al-ʿUbāb] Alobab, that is, The Universe. But القيق [al-qīq] alkik is the crow. Damir describes it thus: القيق طاير علي قدر اليمامة واهل الشام يسمونه ابو زريق وهو الوف للناس فيه قبول للتعليم وسرعة ادراك لما يعلم ويحاكي كلما يسمع وقد تقدم الكلام [col. 293] عليه في باب الزاي المعجمة [al-qīq ṭāyir ʿalī qadr al-yamāma wa-ahl al-Shām yusammūnahu abū zurayq wa-huwa alūf li-l-nās fīhi qabūl li-l-taʿlīm wa-surʿat idrāk li-mā yuʿallam wa-yuḥākī kullamā yasmaʿ wa-qad taqaddama al-kalām ʿalayhi fī bāb al-zāy al-muʿjama] Alkik is a bird approaching the size of a turtledove, which is called by the inhabitants of Syria abu-zarik (that is, the grey-blue father). It lives with people. It has a capacity for learning and ease in grasping what it is taught. And it repeats whatever it hears. But it has already been dealt with in the chapter on Ze. That is, under the word زاغ [zāgh] Zag, which is the common name of the crow, although others explain it as the magpie ^{R1} Since, then, the bird [III, 41] named קיק kik differs so from the bird קוק kuk, they ought not to have been confused ^{R2}.

But those Talmudists are also gravely mistaken who will have שמן קיק, oleum kik [kik oil], taken from a bird, since it is κίκινον ἔλαιον [kikinon elaion], that is, oil pressed from the seeds of the plant which the Egyptians called KIKI` [kiki]. Many ancient writers mention it. Thus Herodotus, book 1, chapter 92, says that the marsh-dwelling Egyptians use an ointment ἀπὸ τῶν σιλλικυπρίων τοῦ καρποῦ, τὸ καλεῦσι μὲν Αἰγύπτιοι KIKI` [apo tōn sillikypriōn tou karpou, to kaleusi men Aigyptioi kiki], from the fruit of the syllicyprium, which the Egyptians call KIKI. And Strabo, book 17, in his description of Egypt: Καὶ τὸ KIKKI` (read KIKI`) καρπός τις σπειρόμενος ἐν ἀρούραις, ἐξ οὗ ἔλαιον ἀποθλίβεται [Kai to kikki … karpos tis speiromenos en arourais, ex hou elaion apothlibetai]. And KIKI is a certain fruit, sown in the fields, from which oil is pressed. And Dioscorides, book 4: KIKI`, ἢ κρότων [kiki, ē krotōn], etc. ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον [ex hou apothlibetai to legomenon kikinon elaion]. And Pliny, book 15, chapter 7: Oil is also made from the CICI tree, abundant in Egypt. Hence Hesychius: Κίκη· φυτόν [Kikē· phyton]; but it should be corrected to Κικί [Kiki]. And this is the very kikajon קיקיון of Jonah, and the elcheroa الخروع [al-kharwaʿ] of the Arabs. This was already observed by Jerome nearly thirteen hundred years ago. For the gourd, or ivy (he says on Jonah) we read in the Hebrew קיקיון, which in the Syriac and Punic language is also called elkeroa. Accordingly, in the Coptic Lexicon ^{a)} the Egyptian word KOYKI` [kouki] kuki [III, 42] (for which I would write KIKI` [kiki]) is rendered in Arabic حب الخروع [ḥabb al-kharwaʿ], the seed of elcheroa or alcheroa. And in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār], in the chapter خروع [kharwaʿ] cheroa, the words of Dioscorides on κικὶ [kiki], ἐξ οὗ ἀποθλίβεται τὸ λεγόμενον κίκινον ἔλαιον [ex hou apothlibetai to legomenon kikinon elaion], are rendered in Arabic thus: ومنها يتعصر الدهن المسمي قيقي وهو دهن الخروع [wa-minhā yutaʿaṣṣar al-duhn al-musammī qīqī wa-huwa duhn al-kharwaʿ], And from it is pressed the oil which they call the oil KIKI, which is the oil ALCHEROA. Indeed there are even some among the Talmudists for whom kik, from which the oil comes, is the same as kikajon. The Talmud, in the place cited above: ריש לקיש אמר קיקיון דיונה אמר רבה בר בר חנה לדידי חזי לי קיקיון דיונה ולצלוליבה דמי, Resh Lakish said: It is the kikajon of Jonah. Rabba Bar son of Hana said: As for me, I have seen the kikajon of Jonah, and it is a plant resembling the selulibah. Indeed it is the same, if selulibah is truly the alcheroa الخروع [al-kharwaʿ] of the Arabs, as is found in the Responsa of the Geonim, that is, of the illustrious doctors, where seluliba is defined: אילן סרק יש במקומינו ועושה גרעינים ועושין מהן שמן ומין סממנין וכל מי שיש בו צנה הרבה שותה ממנו ושמו בלשון ערבי אלכרו״ע ושמנו קורין דהן כרוע, A barren tree growing in our lands, bearing seeds from which oil is made, and a kind of red colouring. And whoever is seized by a severe chill drinks of this oil. In Arabic it is called alcheroa, and its oil the oil cheroa. So Baal Aruch [=the ʿArukh of Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome] [=Nathan ben Jehiel of Rome, the ʿArukh] cites it. But in Kimchi's Commentaries, where this same passage is quoted, the words ומין סממנין, and a kind of red colouring, appear nowhere. [col. 294] I therefore suspect that they were either added from elsewhere or corrupted, and that in their place we should read ומין שמשומין, and a kind of sesame, so that seliluba, or alcheroa, is said to be among the kinds of sesame, an opinion held by some of the ancients. Pliny, book 15, chapter 7, on manufactured oil: Next is that made from the CICI tree, abundant in Egypt; some call it croton, others trixis (or rather sili, as Salmasius [=Claude Saumaise (1588–1653), Plinianae exercitationes] on Solinus would have it read), others wild sesame. The Supplement to Dioscorides: Κικὶ, ἢ κρότων, οἱ δὲ σήσαμον ἄγριον [Kiki, ē krotōn, hoi de sēsamon agrion]. The Arabic Pandectarius: CICI of Dioscorides, or wild sesame, etc., kerva in Arabic. It should also be noted that in Herodotus it is called τὰ σιλλικύπρια [ta sillikypria], in the Supplement to Dioscorides σεσελὶ κύπριον [seseli kyprion], and in Pliny sili, words which seem to allude to the barbarian seluliba ^{R3}. But this in passing; now to the matter at hand.

[III, 43] Both the Arabs and the Talmudists have taught us that the Hebrew קאת kaath is the same as קוק huk and kuk, a water bird with a long neck. But since this is not enough, because there are many water birds with long necks, the Greeks and Jerome point us to the pelican; and I gladly embrace this rendering as the truest. For the origin of the word leads us to it, which plainly derives from the verb קאה kaah, that is, to vomit. Hence Baal Hatturim [=Jacob ben Asher (d. 1343), commentary on the Torah]: הקאת דרכו להקיא מאכלו, "the kaath is accustomed to vomit up its food." And lest the final Tav be thought an obstacle, Rabbi Jonah teaches that it is a formative of the noun, and that the true root is קאה kaah. And Kimchi cites a poet who says קאות kaoth in the plural. So, just as from פרה comes פרת for the Euphrates, and שחת, pit, from שחה, so קאת, pelican, comes from קאה ^{R4}. And why it is named from vomiting is not obscure to those who know that the pelican brings back up shells it has already swallowed, after they have been opened by the heat of its belly, so as to pick out the edible parts from them. The ancient writers assert this with such agreement that the matter cannot be called into doubt. Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 10: Οἱ δὲ πελεκᾶνες, οἱ ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γινόμενοι, καταπίνουσι τὰς μεγάλας κόγχας καὶ λείας· ὅταν δὲ ἐν τῷ πρὸ τῆς κοιλίας τόπῳ πέψωσιν, ἐξεμοῦσιν, ἵνα χασκουσῶν τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντες ἐσθίωσι. [Hoi de pelekanes, hoi en tois potamois ginomenoi, katapinousi tas megalas konchas kai leias; hotan de en tō pro tēs koilias topō pepsōsin, exemousin, hina chaskousōn ta krea exaphountes esthiōsi.] "River pelicans swallow large smooth shells, and when these have been cooked in the stomach they vomit them up, so as to take the flesh out of them as they gape and eat it." And in the book of Marvels [ch. 13]: Φασὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας τὰς ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς γενομένας κόγχας ὀρύττοντας κατεσθίειν· ἔπειτα, ὅταν πλῆθος εἰσφορήσωσιν αὐτῶν, ἐξεμεῖν, εἶθ᾽ οὕτως τὰ μὲν κρέα ἐσθίειν τῶν κογχῶν, τῶν δὲ ὀστράκων μὴ ἅπτεσθαι. [Phasi tous pelekanas tas en tois potamois genomenas konchas oryttontas katesthiein; epeita, hotan plēthos eisphorēsōsin autōn, exemein, eith' houtōs ta men krea esthiein tōn konchōn, tōn de ostrakōn mē haptesthai.] "They say that pelicans devour shells dug out of the rivers, and, having taken in a quantity of them, soon vomit them up, so that they pick out the flesh to eat and leave the shells alone." Antigonus of Carystus, Story 47: Τοὺς δὲ πελεκᾶνας τὰς θηλείας κόγχας καταπίνειν ἱστορεῖ· ἔπειτα ὀλίγας κατασχόντας ἐν τῷ ἄνω τῆς κοιλίας ἐξεμεῖν κεχηνυίας· εἶτα οὕτω τὰ κρέα ἐξαφοῦντας ἐσθίειν. [Tous de pelekanas tas thēleias konchas katapinein historei; epeita oligas kataschontas en tō anō tēs koilias exemein kechēnuias; eita houtō ta krea exaphountas esthiein.] This suffers from three errors: for τὰς θηλείας κόγχας [tas thēleias konchas], female shells, read τὰς λείας κόγχας [tas leias konchas], smooth shells, as in Aristotle; for ἱστορεῖ [historei], he relates, read ἱστορεῖται [historeitai], it is related; and for ὀλίγας κατασχόντας [oligas kataschontas], having retained small ones, read ὀλίγον κατασχόντας [oligon kataschontas], having retained them a little while. It should therefore be translated thus: "It is related that pelicans swallow smooth shells; then, [III, 44] after retaining them a little while in the top of the stomach, they vomit them up gaping, and so take out the flesh and eat it." Pliny, book 10, chapter 40: "The same bird, when it has filled itself with swallowed shells, vomits them up cooked by the heat of its belly, and so picks out the edible parts from them, rejecting the shells." Aelian, History of Animals, book 3, chapter 20: Οἱ πελεκᾶνες, ἐν τοῖς ποταμοῖς κόγχας περιχαίνοντες· εἶτα καταπίνουσιν· ἔνδον δὲ καὶ ἐν μυχῷ τῆς γαστρὸς ὑποθάλψαντες ἀνεμοῦσιν, καὶ τὰ μὲν ὀστράκια ἐκ τῆς ἀλέας διέστη ὡσπεροῦν τῶν ἑφθῶν. οἱ δὲ ἐξορύττουσι τὰ κρέα, καὶ ἔχουσι δεῖπνον. [Hoi pelekanes, en tois potamois konchas perichainontes; eita katapinousin; endon de kai en mychō tēs gastros hypothalpsantes anemousin, kai ta men ostrakia ek tēs aleas diestē hōsperoun tōn hephthōn. hoi de exoryttousi ta krea, kai echousi deipnon.] "Spoonbills gape after river shells and swallow them; and having warmed them in the depth of the stomach they vomit them up. And from the shells, forced apart by the heat of the belly, as if they had been cooked, they dig out the flesh for food." Almost the same is found in Apostolius, Century 15, Proverb 93. Eustathius on the Hexaemeron, after saying that the shells they swallow are loosened by the heat of the throat, says: ἐξεμέσαντες οὖν αὐτὰς εὐμαρῶς τὸ ἐδώδιμον αὐτῶν [exemesantes oun autas eumarōs to edōdimon autōn] [col. 295] κατεσθίουσιν [katesthiousin], "having vomited them up, they easily eat what is edible." Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)], On Animals, chapter 8:

Κόγχην δὲ πελεκὰν ἐμβαλὼν τοῖς ἐγκάτοις, Κἀνάπαλιν αὐτὴν ἐξενεγκὼν ὀστράκοις Τὸ σαρκίον βέβρωκε ληφθὲν εὐστόχως. [Konchēn de pelekan embalōn tois enkatois, Kanapalin autēn exenenkōn ostrakois To sarkion bebrōke lēphthen eustochōs.]

"The pelican, having sent a shell down into its innards and brought it back up again, skilfully feeds on the flesh taken out of the shell." Pisides too, On the Creation of the World, says that they send the shells down into the fire of their innards, since they cannot be opened otherwise:

Λύσιν δὲ πάσχει τῶν πτυχῶν ἡ στεῤῥότης, Τῇ θερμότητι τῶν ἔσω χαυνουμένη. Θᾶττον δὲ τὰς πρὶν ἐξεμοῦντες συνδέσεις, Γυμνῇ διαρπάζουσι τὰς σάρκας μάχῃ, Τὴν ὀστρακώδη μὴ φορούσας ἀσπίδα. [Lysin de paschei tōn ptychōn hē sterrotēs, Tē thermotēti tōn esō chaunoumenē. Thatton de tas prin exemountes syndeseis, Gymnē diarpazousi tas sarkas machē, Tēn ostrakōdē mē phorousas aspida.]

Then the firmness of the valves gives way, loosened by the inner heat. And soon, vomiting up what had previously been bound shut, they tear apart the flesh, no longer protected by its shelly shield, in an unequal fight. It must be admitted, however, that Plutarch, in the book Utra anim., attributes this same thing to herons, when he says that the art of opening oysters is owed τοῖς ἐρωδίων σοφίσμασιν· ὅταν γὰρ τὴν κόγχην καταπίῃ μεμυκυῖαν, ἐνοχλούμενος ἐγκαρτερεῖ, μέχρις ἂν αἴσθηται μαλασσομένην, καὶ χαλῶσαν ὑπὸ τῆς θερμότητος· τότε δὲ ἐκβαλὼν κεχηνυῖαν, καὶ ἀπεσπασμένην, ἐξεῖλε τὸ ἐδώδιμον [tois erōdiōn sophismasin; hotan gar tēn konchēn katapiē memykuian, enochloumenos enkarterei, mechris an aisthētai malassomenēn, kai chalōsan hypo tēs thermotētos; tote de ekbalōn kechēnuian, kai apespasmenēn, exeile to edōdimon], to the ingenuity of herons: for when the heron has swallowed a closed shell, although it finds it troublesome, it nevertheless endures it until it feels it softened and loosened by the heat; then, casting it out gaping and torn open, it takes the edible part out of it. And Aelian, book 3, chapter 24, after relating that storks offer their own food, vomited up, to their young if nothing else is available with which to feed them, adds καὶ τοὺς ἐρωδίους ποιεῖν [III, 45] ταὐτὸ, καὶ τοὺς πελεκᾶνας μέντοι [kai tous erōdious poiein tauto, kai tous pelekanas mentoi], that herons too, and pelicans, do the same. But what we have said about pelicans is celebrated by constant report and by everyone's talk, whereas what Plutarch and Aelian write about herons and storks is very obscure, and has no other authorities, as far as I remember. Indeed, I would think that by the name herons Plutarch means pelicans, which many count among the herons, because the pelican differs from the heron almost only in its bill, which it has broader at the tip and in the shape of a spoon ^{R5}. Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium]: It certainly seems to me that our pelican should be counted in the heron kind, from which it differs not so much by any other mark as by the breadth of its bill. Likewise: Albertus also thought that the bird which we call the spoonbill (that is, the pelican) was the white heron. Turner [=William Turner, Avium praecipuarum historia (1544)]: If I had not seen the albardeola (that is, the white heron) in Italy, I would have judged the English shovelard (that is, the pelican) to be the albardeola. For Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] too, book 4 De Avibus, chapter 5, Aristotle's λευκερώδιος [leukerōdios] (that is, white heron) is the bird which from the shape of its bill they call pale poche ou cullier, that is, the pelican of the ancients. Plutarch, therefore, could on the same grounds take herons and pelicans indiscriminately. Or, if it is true that the heron too, like the pelican, vomits up shells ^{R6}, as Plutarch holds, why could the Hebrew name קאת kaath, formed from vomiting, not have been common to the heron and the pelican, since they are kindred birds and alike in so many respects?

Granting this, these words of the Psalmist, Ps 102:7, will be plainer: Because of the voice of my groaning my bones have cleaved to my flesh; I have become like the kaath of the wilderness; I have been like the chos of the desolate places. In these he compares himself, on account of his laments and groans, to two birds, namely the kaath and the chos. From this one may infer that these birds have something plaintive and groaning about them. And among the many reasons which almost persuade us that the chos is the onocrotalus, this was one: that the onocrotalus is a bird of dreadful voice, which admirably imitates the wailing of a man in grievous pain. [III, 46] Accordingly, so that the Psalmist be consistent, the same must be shown of the bird kaath too. This will be difficult if kaath means nothing but the pelican, since nothing whatever is found about the voice of the pelican. But if the name kaath is common to the heron and the pelican, [col. 296] which I think agrees with the truth, it will be easy to find a way out. For the heron has a loud voice ^{R7}. Homer calls it a clangor, and in Iliad 10 he says of the heron which Pallas sent as a favourable omen to Diomedes and Ulysses as they went by night to the enemy camp:
— — — τοὶ δ' οὐ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι Νύκτα δι' ὀρφναίην, ἀλλὰ κλάγξαντος ἄκουσαν· [— — — toi d' ou idon ophthalmoisi / Nykta di' orphnaiēn, alla klanxantos akousan;]

They did not see it with their eyes through the dark night, but heard it clanging. And the Philosopher, on the ash-coloured heron, History book 9, chapter 1: Τούτων (ἐρωδίων) ὁ πέλλος χαλεπῶς εὐνάζει τε, καὶ ὀχεύει. κράζει τε γὰρ, καὶ αἷμα, ὥς φασιν, ἀφίησιν ἐκ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ὀχεύων, καὶ τίκτει φαυλῶς, ὡς καὶ ὀδυνηρῶς. [Toutōn (erōdiōn) ho pellos chalepōs eunazei te, kai ocheuei. krazei te gar, kai haima, hōs phasin, aphiēsin ek tōn ophthalmōn ocheuōn, kai tiktei phaulōs, hōs kai odynērōs.] Which Pliny, book 1, chapter 60, renders thus: These suffer anguish in coupling. The males indeed shed blood from their eyes with loud cries; nor do the females give birth with less difficulty. But, what is most to be noted, the starry heron, or stellaris, which is commonly called the butaurus [bittern], is a bird whose bellowing is so dreadful that in this respect it scarcely yields to the onocrotalus. It is strange that the ancients were silent about this, unless these words of Pliny, book 10, chapter 42, refer to it: There is one that imitates the lowing of oxen in the territory of Arles, called the bull. And those of the author of the Philomela:
And in the marshy waters the butio booms.

However that may be, nothing is better known than the booming of this bird; yet for the benefit of the less learned, here are passages about it from more recent writers! Vincent, in the Doctrinale, book 16, ch. 151: The butorius is a bird so called from the sound of its voice, etc. Instead of a song it utters a terrifying cry. And it is said to be unable to do this unless it plunges its head into the water, so that the density of the element makes the voice it has formed within resound like a kind of thunder. Albertus: It utters a horrible sound like a horn, thrusting its bill into the mud of the marsh, so that its voice bursts forth in it like thunder. Yet it sits on the banks of lakes and marshes, where, putting its bill into the water, it produces such booms that it can easily be heard a mile away, an Italian mile. Belon, On Birds, book 4, chapter 4: When it comes upon the bank of a pool or marsh, it puts its bill into the water and produces so great a sound that no ox could bellow with so strained a voice. And the neighbouring places resound so that it is heard half a league away. [III, 47] Gesner: It is said to put its bill into the water and to raise a very great noise at the bottom of the water, with a strained voice like a bull's, which can be heard almost half a German mile away (that is, an hour's journey). A learned man, in a letter to Gesner describing the butorius under the name onocrotalus, writes: When it wishes to give voice, it either plunges its bill, which is long, into the water or sticks it into the bank. It does this after sunset, and often continues its booming the whole night. Hence the Italians call it trombono, from the sound of a trumpet, and tarabusa or terrabusa, because it pierces the earth with its bill and utters a horrible sound. For its German names, taken from the same source, see Gesner ^{R8}. Thus Beza, not wrongly taking קאת kaath for the bittern, rendered the words of the Psalmist thus:
Ie suis au butor semblable Du desert inhabitable.

This surprises me all the more because he had no one to follow. For the Greeks, Jerome and Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] had rendered it pelican, Munster hoopoe, Arias [=Benito Arias Montano, the interlinear Latin of the Antwerp Polyglot] cuckoo, Castalio [=Sebastian Castellio, Latin Bible (1551)] onocrotalus, and in the Law ibis, and the Genevans cormorant, that is, phalacrocorax.

But, you will say, whether by the name קאת kaath you understand the heron or the pelican, why is it placed in deserts, when it is said in the Psalm, I am become like כקאת מדבר, the kaath of the desert; and in Isa 34:11. And the kaath and the hedgehog shall possess it; and in Soph. II, 14. Both the kaath and the hedgehog in its upper storeys, passages that deal with the desolation of Idumaea and Assyria? Is it right to assign to water birds, such as the pelican and the heron, a dwelling in desert and waterless places? Whoever published the Commentaries on the Psalms under the name of Jerome answers that there are two kinds of these birds, of which one lives in [col. 297] the waters, and its food is fish; and the other in the wilderness, and its food is venomous animals, that is, serpents, crocodiles and lizards. But there is no need to take refuge in this, since not every desert is waterless. In the interior of Marmarica, a region that is extremely desert, Ptolemy places the marsh of Cleartes, the marsh of Laccus and the marsh of Lycomedes. In the deserts of Arabia the Israelites came upon the waters of Marah and the springs of Elim, Exod 15:23 27. Those, therefore, are mistaken who think that water birds nowhere find a suitable habitation in deserts ^{R9}.

notes.text: It seems rather to be the sturnus [starling].
notes.label: R1

notes.text: This, however, is exactly what J. E. Faber [=J. E. Faber, notes to the German edition of Harmer's Observations (Beobachtungen über den Orient, 1772–79)] did in his dissertation de Animalibus, quorum mentio sit Zephan. II, 14 (Göttingen 1769; reprinted at the end of Cramer's book entitled Scythische Denkmaeler in Palaestina), where he contends that قيق [qyq], قوق [qwq], ܩܩܐ [קקא], קיק, קוק, קקא and קקתא are names of a single bird, the cornix [crow], differing from one another only in spelling. But even if the Hebrew masters sometimes take קוק and קיק indiscriminately for the crow, it is nevertheless clear from what Bochart has adduced from Damir that the Arabic قيق [qyq] and قوق [qwq] differ from each other; and that the Syriac ܩܩܐ [קקא] designates the pelican is clearly taught by the Physiologus Syrus edited by Tychsen, ch. 20, pp. 13 and 110, and by Tychsen himself, pp. 111–114. The Syriac name of the crow is rather ܩܘܪܩܣܐ [קורקסא] Korakso, which arose from the sound and is the Greek κόραξ [korax]; see the same Physiolog. Syr. Chapter 24. Faber, therefore, interprets the Hebrew word as the crow on the authority of the Arabic translator in the Polyglots alone, who puts قيق [qyq] for קאת. Schoder copied Faber in Specim. Hieroz. II, Tit. 9. But in truth the crow in no way fits the passages of the Psalms and Zephaniah. For Zephaniah II, 14 places the קאת among the ruins and deserted places of the cities of Nineveh and Zion, whereas the crow frequents the surroundings of cities and houses; and David, Ps 102:7, compares his weeping with the laments and groans of the קאת; yet no one, so far as I know, has ever yet heard laments from a crow. Moreover, Moses in Lev 11:18 has already included the crow under the genus of ravens, ערב, so that there was no need to name this bird separately, as Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] aptly points out, fasc. 3, Chapter 6, p. 58.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: Add what our author will discuss below, book 4, ch. 27, p. 623. That the Hebrew קיקיון, the Arabic الخروع [al-khirwaʿ], and the Egyptian Kiki is the ricinus vulgaris or medicus, French Palme de Christ, German der Wunderbaum, is shown by Celsius [=Olof Celsius, Hierobotanicon (1745-47)] in Hierobot. vol. 2, pp. 273–282, and Michaelis [=J. D. Michaelis (1717–91), orientalist: Supplementa ad lexica hebraica; Fragen an eine Gesellschaft gelehrter Männer] in Supplemm. vol. 6, p. 2185 ff. Compare Niebuhr's [=Carsten Niebuhr, Beschreibung von Arabien (1772)] Descript. Arab. p. 148 and Forsskål's [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)] Flora Aegyptio-Arabica, pp. 164, 75, 121.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: To Michaelis, in Supplemm. ad Lexx. [=J. D. Michaelis, Supplementa ad lexica Hebraica] Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2158, the letter ת does not seem to be a feminine ending but part of the root; for from the root קיא, to vomit, one could indeed form קאה, but not קאת. But Michaelis did not consider that the word קאת must be derived from קאה, to vomit out, which occurs in Lev 18:28, and that there are some nouns derived from verbs with quiescent third He which usually take the letter Thau in the place and function of the third radical, such as the nouns Bochart listed above, to which may be added שפת, lip, דלת, door, קשת, bow, from שפה, דלה, קשה, etc. Cf. Schroeder, Institt. ad fundamenta Ling. Hebr. sect. 7, rule 106 β, p. 135.
notes.label: R4

notes.text: He means the Platalea Leucorodia of Linnaeus (Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 2, p. 613, ed. Gmelin [=J. F. Gmelin, 13th edition of Linnaeus, Systema naturae (1788–93)]). But what the ancients relate in their tales about their πελεκανος [pelekanos] does not fit the Platalea: that this bird loves its young so much that, whenever food is lacking, it wounds its own breast with its beak so that they may not die of hunger, and gives them the flowing blood to drink. How the Platalea could wound itself with its broad bill is hard to understand. J. D. Michaelis, in the Quaestiones proposed to those travelling to Arabia, no. 100, p. 331, in the Nott. ad Vernacul. on Levit. XI, and in Supplemm. ad Lexx. Hebrr. vol. 6, p. 2158, takes the πελεκαν [pelekan] of the ancient authors for the onocrotalus of the moderns. But Oedmann rightly points out, fasc. 3, p. 60, that for the ancients themselves the onocrotalus and the pelican are different birds (see also our author above, Chapter 20, p. 275), whereas everything the ancients relate about the pelican is found in the Pelecanus Graculus of Linnaeus (Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 574), of which he also added a picture.
notes.label: R5

notes.text: That the Pelecanus Graculus also vomits up fish was observed by Georgi, cited by Oedmann (3, p. 61).
notes.label: R6

notes.text: By the heron Bochart means the stellaris, called Butor by the French, Bittour or Bittern by the English, Rohrdommel by the Germans. See Linnaeus, Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 635 f.
notes.label: R7

notes.text: And in Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)], Ornithol. vol. 3, book 20, Chapter 16, p. 403, from Gesner.
notes.label: R8

notes.text: You see how uncertainly Bochart wavers between the pelican and the bittern. Nor would I think that anything certain can be put forward today about the bird קאת. [III, 48] For the ancient interpreters disagree; the etymology fits several birds; and what occurs in the Hebrew Codex about קאת is not so peculiar to one particular genus of birds that, among very different ones, no room for doubt is left. For there are many water birds (if indeed קאת is a water bird) which inhabit marshy deserts and utter a cry that is either plaintive and moaning or dreadful and clanging (Oedmann, moreover, says nothing about the voice of his Pelecanus graculus). — Among the Arabs, كعيت [kuʿayt] also occurs among the names of the nightingale. Hence Velthusen [=J. C. Velthusen, in Symbolae litterariae Kilonienses], in Part 2 of the Symbolae Kilonienses, edited in the vernacular by Cramer (Beyträge zur Beförderung theologischer und anderer nützlicher Kenntnisse), thinks that the Hebrew קאת is to be interpreted in Ps 102:7 as the solitary nightingale, and in Esaj. XXXIV, 11. and Zeph 2:14 as the phoenicurus or ruticilla [redstart] (rossignol de muraille, de roc, ou de rocher, see Salerne, Ornithol. p. 233), which nests in the hollows of walls and of the back parts of houses, where people are less frequent (see Jonston, Theatr. animall., Frankfurt 1755, vol. 1, p. 125). But although the Arabs sometimes put the letter ك for the Hebrew ק (as in ضحك [ḍaḥika], Hebr. צחק, and كدر [kadira], Hebr. קדר), and ع for the Hebrew א (as كعب [kaʿaba], Hebr. כעב and כאב, he filled), such examples are nevertheless rare, and it is quite unusual for both Hebrew letters ק and א to stand in one and the same word for the Arabic ك and ع. — Jo. Christoph. Doederlein, in his Scholia on Ps 102:7, explains קאת as the viverra Zibetha or wild cat, comparing the Arabic قط البر [qiṭṭ al-barr], i.e. wild cat, in Forsskål, Descript. Animall. p. 1, no. 7, letter b. But, to say nothing of the fact that the Hebrew קאת has nothing in common with the Arabic قط [qiṭṭ] except the sound, one cannot think of a mammalian quadruped for the reason that קאת appears among the birds in Lev 11:18 and Deut 14:17.
notes.label: R9
